segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Isha in the original: three moods in half a verse, and svid, the raised eyebrow. Whose, I wonder, is wealth? The second verse picks up right there.

Every so often a video goes around: someone quits everything and moves to a cabin with no signal, and the comments fill up with people wishing they could too. It's a real pull, especially in a heavy week. The Isha's second verse has a word for the opposite of the cabin: iha, here. Except, read the line, kurvann eveha karmani, and you can't find it. Here has vanished. It didn't leave. It got swallowed, and getting it back is today's reading.
screen: `QUIT EVERYTHING. MOVE TO A CABIN.` → `IHA: HERE.` → `SWALLOWED, NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: The whole line: kurvann eveha karmani jijivishet shatam samah. Kurvann eveha is three words run together: kurvan, doing; eva, just or indeed; iha, here. When eva meets iha, the a and the i melt into one e, and here disappears inside eveha. That's sandhi, the joining of sounds, from earlier this year, working in a living line. Doing, just here. Not somewhere quieter. Here. Next, karmani: works, actions, the plural of karma. Then a verb that wants something. The root is jiv, to live. Jijivishet doubles the start, ji-jiv, adds a hiss, and that shape means wanting to. So not live, but may one wish to live. Shatam samah: a hundred years. The text says it plainly. The second line gives the reason: na karma lipyate nare. Lipyate is is smeared, the way mud or oil gets smeared on. Nare: on a person. Action is not smeared on a person. Put it back together and the verse is a whole life in two lines. Doing works, just here, may one wish to live a hundred years; so, and no other way, the work doesn't stick. For a heavy week, that's a different answer from the cabin. Not less doing. Doing that doesn't cling.
screen: `KURVANN EVEHA: DOING, JUST HERE.` · `JIJIVISHET: MAY ONE WISH TO LIVE.` · `LIPYATE: SMEARED ON.` · `THE WORK DOESN'T STICK.`

segments.voice: Rest both hands, palms up, on your lap, and notice them: the hands that did today's work. On each out-breath, let what they've done slide off like water off an oiled pan, while the hands stay warm and ready. If you pray, you can offer the day's work as it slides away.
Reading the Isha in the original, verse two: kurvann eveha, doing, just here, with here hiding inside a join, and jijivishet, a verb that wishes to live.

notes: Year one, day 234, taught this verse's meaning; this day reads its sandhi (kurvan + eva + iha) and the desiderative jijivishet.
Grammar to confirm: eva + iha → eveha; jijivishet as the optative of the desiderative of jiv; lipyate as passive 'is smeared'; nare as locative 'on a person'.
'Sandhi … from earlier this year' points back to the year-five days on sandhi (around 1451–1462); adjust if those lessons are worded differently.
The second line's middle (nanyatheto 'sti) is paraphrased as 'so, and no other way'.
howItsDone pairs the verse with the Gita's teaching on action ('often'); soften if needed.
